extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate or graduate students in communication / mass media studies (readers of an introductory communication theory textbook)
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter summarizing agenda-setting theory: its definitions, core assumptions, models (levels), mechanisms (accessibility/priming/framing), variants (agenda-building, agenda-cutting, agenda-melding), empirical findings, contingencies, critiques, and directions for future research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda
rubrics_metrics.description: “the list of important issues” — the items considered salient in public discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the basic object of study in agenda-setting: media attention determines which issues appear on the agenda and how they are ranked. (Note: the page distinguishes agenda as media, public, and policy agendas — see separate entries.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Media framing
rubrics_metrics.description: “the way the messages are depicted, the way ideas are organized and presented.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing influences interpretation via choices such as headline size, photos, story length, and story positioning; affects how messages are interpreted and can determine the perspective through which issues are understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priming
rubrics_metrics.description: “what the media present influences what we think about later.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposure to certain issues or attributes increases the likelihood that those considerations will be used in later evaluations (e.g., of political candidates or policies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Media agenda
rubrics_metrics.description: “priority placed by media” — the issues emphasized and prioritized by news organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media agenda is the source in classical agenda-setting chains; its prominence (frequency, placement, prominence) drives public accessibility of issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public agenda
rubrics_metrics.description: “result of media agenda interacting with public agenda” — the set of issues the public perceives as important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public agenda arises from media effects plus interpersonal communication and real-world cues; it mediates influence on policy agenda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy agenda
rubrics_metrics.description: “result of public agenda interacting with policymakers” — issues taken up by policymakers and institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy agenda can be shaped by media and public agendas, but also by elite sources and institutional processes; scholars distinguish policy agenda-setting from agenda-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core assumption 1: The media establish an agenda
rubrics_metrics.description: The media do not just report reality but filter and shape it; they establish which issues are salient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the foundational claim: repeated and prominent coverage makes issues more accessible in public memory and thus perceived as more important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core assumption 2: Media confer salience
rubrics_metrics.description: “The media give importance, or salience, to its topics. The more the media focuses on certain issues, the more likely the public perceives such issues as important.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Salience is measured by frequency, prominence, and prominence cues; persistent coverage over time increases perceived importance (issue saliency).

rubrics_metrics.name: Core assumption 3: Reciprocity in agenda influence
rubrics_metrics.description: “The public and policymakers have the ability to influence the media’s agenda.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agenda-setting is not purely top-down; agenda-building emphasizes reciprocal influences among media, public, and elites (e.g., press releases, social media, elite sourcing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda-setting process (accessibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agenda-setting occurs through a cognitive process known as “accessibility” — frequency and prominence of coverage influence how accessible issues are in memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accessibility explains why respondents name the most covered news issues as the country’s top problems; the effect is cumulative across many messages rather than single exposures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness model
rubrics_metrics.description: One of McCombs' three models: an issue is on an individual's agenda because they have seen it in the media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If media do not report an issue, individuals are unlikely to be aware of it; awareness depends on exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priorities model
rubrics_metrics.description: One of McCombs' models: issues the media prioritize will likely be prioritized by individuals as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media prioritization leads audiences to allocate attention and concern to the same issues, even when other issues may be objectively more pressing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salience model
rubrics_metrics.description: A model between awareness and priorities: media-presented issues appear on individuals’ agendas but not to the same extent as media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals’ agendas reflect media emphasis to varying degrees; some issues align closely while others show weaker transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-level agenda-setting (object salience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on which issues or objects (e.g., topics, public figures) are made salient by media coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic agenda-setting research compares salience of news content with public perceptions (e.g., Chapel Hill study).

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-level agenda-setting (attribute agenda-setting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on how the media influence which attributes of issues/people are salient (i.e., “how to think about” an issue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Second-level concerns selection of attributes (substantive vs. affective) and is sometimes framed as overlapping with framing; it shifts attention from issue salience to attribute salience and valence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-level agenda-setting vs. framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate whether framing is part of second-level agenda-setting or a distinct process (differences: accessibility vs. attribution; issue importance vs. interpretation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weaver/McCombs see framing as extension of agenda-setting (selecting salient attributes); Scheufele argues framing and agenda-setting operate via different cognitive processes and outcomes. Guidance: distinguish functions in news production, news processing, and locus of effect when analyzing studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-level agenda-setting / Network Agenda Setting Model
rubrics_metrics.description: The news media can transfer the salience of relationships among sets of elements so audiences perceive elements as interconnected (bundled).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third-level examines networks of associations (how topics and attributes are linked in public minds) rather than linear salience; empirical work looks at co-occurrence patterns and perceived linkages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contingency conditions: Relevance and Uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Two variables that condition agenda-setting effects: relevance (motivation to seek orientation) and uncertainty (how much information people think they have).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relevance is high and uncertainty is high, people are more likely to rely on media for orientation. If uncertainty is low (people feel well-informed), media influence is weakened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors affecting media agenda power
rubrics_metrics.description: Media agenda power depends on media credibility, conflicting evidence, shared values between media and public, and the public's need for guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High credibility and shared values increase transfer from media to public; conflicting evidence or low credibility reduce effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience characteristics and obtrusiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Media effects vary by audience pre-existing sensitivities and whether issues are obtrusive (high personal experience) or unobtrusive (low personal experience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtrusive issues (e.g., gas prices) generate public concern even without media; unobtrusive issues are more susceptible to media influence. Audience traits moderate effects (audience-effects model).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda-building
rubrics_metrics.description: Perspective emphasizing interplay among mass media, policymakers, and social processes; recognizes media agenda results from societal influences and actors seeking to shape discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agenda-building highlights reciprocity (media and public affect each other) and the role of sources (press releases, PR, policymakers) in shaping media agendas; scholars study which actors successfully place items on media agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda-melding
rubrics_metrics.description: How individuals join groups and blend their personal agendas with group agendas; forming a collected agenda of issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With the Internet, people form agendas and then find groups with similar agendas; agenda-melding explains group formation and identity via shared agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda-cutting
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to direct attention away from relevant issues by (1) placing an item low on the news agenda (burying it), (2) removing it once it is on the agenda, or (3) completely ignoring it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agenda-cutting is intentional suppression of coverage; mere omission for selection reasons is not the same. Empirical operationalization and theoretical development are limited but growing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet- and social-media-mediated agenda-setting (rippling, diffusion, reversed agenda-setting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three-step process online: (1) internet-mediated agenda-rippling (anonymized opinions spread via blogs/bulletin boards), (2) agenda diffusion (online items get reported and spread), (3) internet-mediated reversed agenda-setting (traditional media pick up online agendas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social media can push issues into the public and media agendas; empirical evidence shows bloggers and online communities sometimes influence mainstream media and policy agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension of emotion / affective agenda-setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotions (especially negative ones) shape attention and political judgment; emotional-affective agendas correspond with public emotional impressions and can be more powerful than cognitive attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affective agenda-setting suggests agenda effects operate not only through cognitive accessibility but also by influencing emotional responses; negative emotions tend to have stronger effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of effects relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Connection between agenda-setting levels and the hierarchy of effects model: first-level corresponds to knowledge (learn), second-level to attitude (feel), and both can influence behavior (do).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers may use agenda-setting to analyze stages of persuasion and which components (knowledge vs. attitude) drive subsequent behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critiques and limitations of agenda-setting theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Common critiques: aggregation of categories inflates correlations; the theory implies a passive audience; effect size varies by issue obtrusiveness and audience characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars address critiques by including audience contingency variables, finer-grained content categories, and studying reciprocal and networked effects (agenda-building, third-level models).
